title: The Sleeve-Shaped Harbor: Hakata Before and After the Grid
standfirst: Hakata traded with the Asian mainland while Kyoto was still building its first palaces, survived two Mongol invasion fleets, and was burned to nothing by retreating samurai in 1586 — only for Toyotomi Hideyoshi to redraw it from scratch a year later. A river was straightened to bury the old harbor; a monk brought back noodles and a festival. This dossier follows the port from its sleeve-shaped inlet to its twin-town grid.

sections.heading: A harbor shaped like a sleeve

paragraphs.text: Long before Hakata had streets, it had an inlet. An Edo-period gazetteer of the district describes a bay that once ran from east of the town westward to the Naka River, curving north then west so that, in the writer's words, it looked like the shape of a sleeve — hence its name, Sode-no-Minato, the Sleeve Harbor. The same book repeats, carefully labeling it a local legend rather than established fact, an old story that the god Susanoo once set out from this very inlet for Silla on the Korean peninsula. Whatever the truth of that tale, the inlet was real, and for centuries it was Hakata's harbor.

It was real enough, in fact, to host one of only three official guesthouses ancient Japan built for foreign envoys. First recorded in 688 as Tsukushi-no-Murotsumi and later renamed Korokan in Chinese style, Fukuoka's guesthouse operated from the late Asuka period into the late Heian period, receiving diplomats, monks and traders from Tang China, Silla and beyond; of the three such halls built at the capital, at Naniwa and here, only this one has been located and excavated. Workers renovating a baseball stadium's outfield stands found the first traces — Chinese and Islamic ceramics and West Asian glassware — in December 1987; the stadium itself came down ten years later so archaeologists could finish the job, and the site became a national historic site in 2004, sharing that status with Fukuoka Castle, whose grounds it shares, in a rare double designation. As official diplomatic missions to the mainland tailed off, Fukuoka City's own account of the site notes, the guesthouse itself changed character, drifting from a formal reception hall into something closer to a private trading post for merchants from Tang China and Silla — an early sign of the pattern this whole district would repeat for the next thousand years.

The district's own name has never been settled with certainty. The same Edo-period gazetteer offers a plain reading — "haku" for broad, open ground and "ta" for a multitude of people, a fitting name for a harbor town — while noting other, more fanciful derivations it declines to fully endorse. What is not in dispute is that a defended checkpoint called Keigo stood somewhere in Hakata from at least as early as the Mongol invasions of the following section, remembered in the gazetteer as functioning "until Ashikaga Takauji's time" before its exact site was lost.

Hakata Bay was also where Japan's most famous foreign invasion broke apart. Kublai Khan's fleets came ashore near here in 1274 and again in 1281; a defensive stone wall the shogunate ordered built along the bay after the first invasion still survives in fragments elsewhere in Fukuoka, and this district's own harbor kept a stranger relic. A 1944 Fukuoka Prefecture survey of Mongol-invasion sites records several stone ships' anchors dredged up, bucket by mechanical bucket, from the floor of Hakata's modern port during harbor-dredging works; the surveyor fixed their positions precisely by compass bearing and tidal depth, and found they lay exactly where the old Sode-no-Minato inlet had opened onto the sea in the thirteenth century, buried under about four feet of mud accumulated since. One anchor, cut from stone quarried in southern Korea, more than seven feet long and crusted with centuries of shell growth, was reckoned by the surveyor to have lain on the seabed for some 666 years, dating it to the first invasion of 1274; a companion piece recovered nearby, made of the same reddish tuff, was donated to the city's own museum.

That particular stone did not stay in a museum case. On 17 December 1940, in a ceremony whose text the same survey reproduces in full, port officials presented it to Miyazaki Shrine — dedicated not to any Mongol-era figure but to the legendary founding emperor, Jimmu, and swept up that same year in a nationwide expansion marking his mythical 2,600th anniversary — with prayers invoking Kublai Khan by name and the "divine wind" that had scattered his ships. The ceremony belongs to its moment — wartime Japan reached eagerly for the story of a foreign fleet destroyed by providence — but the stone itself is a genuine, datable fragment of 1274, recovered from the very ground this district's harbor now occupies.

sections.heading: A monk, a noodle and a vanishing harbor

paragraphs.text: Medieval Hakata's most productive foreign import may have been a Song-dynasty Chinese monk's education. The priest Enni, later honored as Shoichi Kokushi, returned from years of study in China in 1241 and founded the temple of Jotenji the following year; with him, Fukuoka City's own account of the district's food culture holds, came the milling techniques behind udon, soba, manju and yokan, which he is said to have taught to a Hakata teahouse keeper before the recipes spread nationwide with the tea ceremony. Two years after his return, in 1243, the same monk is credited with a stranger legacy still practiced every summer: riding a ritual platform through Hakata's streets, sprinkling purified water to pray away an epidemic, in what the city's own cultural-property records treat as the origin of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival.

Not far from Jotenji stood Shofuku-ji, honored with a plaque in the retired emperor Go-Toba's own hand naming it Japan's first Zen meditation hall; the same gazetteer records that Shofuku-ji's own grounds had once been part of an older complex called Hyakudo, said to have been built by Chinese residents from Song China, so that one Chinese-founded religious site was, in effect, built over by another. Sengai, the eccentric monk-painter still celebrated for his witty, deceptively simple ink paintings, later lived in retirement within Shofuku-ji's grounds.

Between these temples and the merchant quarter, Hakata's medieval prosperity and its harbor's slow disappearance were more connected than they might seem: the same 1921 edition of an old district gazetteer credits the Otomo retainer Usuki Awa-no-kami with straightening the meandering Hie River into a direct channel through the pine groves near these temples in the 1570s — the ancestor of today's Mikasa River — which cut off the water feeding Sode-no-Minato and let the old inlet silt over for good. Villagers digging in the area a century later, the gazetteer notes, still turned up seaweed and shells in what was by then dry ground; by the time Hideyoshi's surveyors arrived two decades after that, the harbor Marco Polo's contemporaries might almost have recognized was already dry land waiting for a name.

Hakata paid for the long Sengoku wars in full. In 1586 the Shimazu clan, occupying the town and hearing of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's approaching army, burned Hakata to the ground as they withdrew. The following year, having conquered Kyushu, Hideyoshi ordered the town rebuilt from nothing, and the result, still known as the Taiko Machiwari, is the grid that much of old Hakata's street plan still follows: his commanders Kuroda Kanbei and Ishida Mitsunari carried out the planning, while the merchants Kamiya Sotan and Shimai Soshitsu — two of the men later remembered as Hakata's three great merchant princes, along with Oga Soku — helped fund and organize the rebuilding. Kushida Shrine, Hakata's guardian shrine since a tradition dates one of its enshrined deities to 757, received Hideyoshi's patronage in the same reconstruction, and its present main hall dates from that campaign. Kamiya Sotan, Hideyoshi's own host in Hakata, and Shimai Soshitsu were not simply local benefactors: both had traded across the Korea Strait and into Southeast Asia for years before the rebuilding, and their capital and connections were as much a part of the Taiko Machiwari's success as Kuroda Kanbei's survey lines. Oga Soku and his son Sohaku, the third of the three merchant princes, are buried, like Sotan, within Shofuku-ji's grounds.

Hakata's merchants kept the town's older, foreign-facing character even after Hideyoshi's rebuilding. When Kuroda Nagamasa took possession of the domain in 1601, his father Kuroda Josui — Hideyoshi's veteran strategist, better known in his own lifetime as Kanbei — lodged for a time in Kamiya Sotan's own Hakata house before Nagamasa built Fukuoka Castle on the Naka River's western bank — founding, in effect, a twin town: merchant Hakata on the river's east side, samurai Fukuoka on its west, sharing a name for the modern city but keeping separate identities for centuries after. Hakata's own Gion-cho neighborhoods were organized into five-household groups in 1612 and given a rotating board of year-officers in 1621, machinery for self-government that outlasted the merchant princes who had first rebuilt the town.

sections.heading: A city burned again, and rebuilt again

paragraphs.text: Hakata's grid survived nearly three and a half centuries before fire returned. On the night of 19 June 1945, 221 American B-29 bombers spent roughly two hours over Fukuoka, burning out an area of some 3.78 square kilometers of the city. The national government's own postwar accounting gives 902 dead, 1,078 injured and 244 more listed missing, with 12,693 households destroyed and the city's water, gas and electricity systems wrecked along with its schools, hospitals and factories.

The same official account that lists the dead also traces the recovery: cleanup and repair began as soon as the war ended, a new Reconstruction Department took over formal rebuilding in January 1946, and by 1949 the city's population had climbed back to roughly 377,000. Almost none of the buildings that stood on Hakata's grid before June 1945 survived that night; what a visitor walks through today, on streets still traceable to the Taiko Machiwari, is a district rebuilt twice from nothing — once by a sixteenth-century warlord's order, once by its own returning residents.

Kushida Shrine still stands where Hideyoshi's carpenters rebuilt it, and every July its precinct fills with the six decorated floats of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa, racing before dawn on the 15th over a course of about four kilometers — a nationally designated Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property since long before UNESCO added it to its own world list in 2016. The festival's documentary trail runs back at least to 1432, when the Kyushu Military Chronicle recorded twelve decorated floats carried through Okinohama during Kushida Shrine's Gion rites; a later, harder-to-verify tradition holds that the Sengoku-era lord Ouchi Yoshitaka divided six of Hakata's own floats off to seed the Gion festival at his own domain capital, Yamaguchi, leaving Hakata with the six floats it has run ever since. A short walk from the shrine, Jotenji keeps its own marker to the udon-and-soba legend Enni is said to have brought home in the thirteenth century, in a temple compound that has stood, rebuilt more than once, on essentially the same ground since 1242.

The Korokan's excavated foundations are laid out for visitors on Fukuoka Castle's grounds today, close enough to the shoreline of Hakata Bay to make the ancient guesthouse's seafront position easy to picture even though the old inlet it once faced is long since built over. Between the shrine, the temple and the excavated foundations, this small district holds physical traces of a foreign guesthouse older than Kyoto's own imperial court records, a fleet the sea itself is said to have destroyed, and a town two different rulers each burned and rebuilt from the ground up.

timeline.what: Tsukushi-no-Murotsumi, later renamed Korokan, is first recorded as a guesthouse for foreign envoys.
One of Kushida Shrine's three enshrined deities is dated by tradition to this year.
The monk Enni returns from Song China and founds Jotenji, reputedly bringing udon- and soba-making methods with him.
Enni's epidemic-prayer procession through Hakata is credited as the origin of the Gion Yamakasa festival.
Mongol invasion fleets land in Hakata Bay; a stone anchor from the first fleet is later dredged from the harbor.
Usuki Awa-no-kami straightens the Hie River, cutting off the water feeding the Sode-no-Minato inlet.
The withdrawing Shimazu clan burns Hakata to the ground.
Toyotomi Hideyoshi orders Hakata rebuilt on a new grid, the Taiko Machiwari.
Kuroda Nagamasa takes the domain; his father Kuroda Josui lodges with the merchant Kamiya Sotan before Nagamasa builds Fukuoka Castle across the river.
Hakata's Gion-cho neighborhoods are organized into five-household groups, then given rotating year-officers.
A dredged Mongol-invasion anchor stone is ceremonially dedicated at Miyazaki Shrine.
An American air raid kills 902 people by the government's own postwar count and burns much of the city.
The Korokan's foundations are discovered, excavated and designated a national historic site.
Hakata Gion Yamakasa is added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

walk.name: Korokan Historic Site and Museum
walk.what: The excavated foundations of Japan's only confirmed ancient diplomatic guesthouse, on the grounds it shares with Fukuoka Castle; imported ceramics and glass found here are on display.

walk.name: Kushida Shrine
walk.what: Hakata's guardian shrine, rebuilt in Hideyoshi's 1587 reconstruction; look for the display float kept year-round and, every July, the six competing Yamakasa themselves.

walk.name: Jotenji
walk.what: Founded in 1242 by the monk Enni; a stone marker inside commemorates the temple's traditional role in bringing udon- and soba-making to Japan.

walk.name: Shofuku-ji
walk.what: Honored by a plaque in Emperor Go-Toba's own hand as Japan's first Zen meditation hall, standing on ground that a local gazetteer says once held an even older Chinese-founded temple complex called Hyakudo.

walk.name: The Reisen neighborhood and the old Hakata grid
walk.what: Streets and block widths here still trace the 1587 Taiko Machiwari grid, laid out after the Shimazu burned the medieval town.

walk.name: The Naka River between Hakata and Fukuoka
walk.what: The river Kuroda Nagamasa chose as the boundary between his new castle town of Fukuoka and the older merchant town of Hakata in 1601, a division the two place names still preserve.

caveats: The Sode-no-Minato inlet's founding legend, involving the god Susanoo sailing to Silla, is presented by the Edo-period gazetteer used here as unverified local tradition, not established history, and is treated the same way in this dossier.

Sources differ by two years on Enni's dates: his return from Song China is dated to 1241, while the epidemic-prayer procession credited as the origin of the Gion Yamakasa festival is dated to 1243; these are treated here as two distinct, sequential events rather than a discrepancy.

This dossier does not give an exact founding year for Shofuku-ji beyond noting its traditional status, confirmed by an imperial plaque, as Japan's first Zen meditation hall; a specific founding date could not be verified from a source opened in this session.

The 1940 dedication ceremony for the Mongol-invasion anchor stone is described here in its wartime context; its Shinto prayer text, which this dossier does not translate in full, reflects the nationalist framing of that specific moment rather than this dossier's own view of the events of 1274.
